items.summary: The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese
items.text:
The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

items.title: Mental Models That Change How You Think | Bill Gurley
items.author: Vicky
items.summary: Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the
items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.title: The Best New Restaurants in Queens
items.summary: Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee
items.text:
Astoria now has a spot to satisfy soulful cravings for long-simmered Korean seolleongtang (ox bone soup). Jin Broth is a takeout counter inside the Marquee Astoria banquet hall, which opened in May. Amid business conventions, there’s marvelous seolleongtang: thick, white, and almost creamy from all the collagen that’s seeped out from hours of simmering beef bones. It comes with the customary fixings of scallions, sea salt, and pepper so everyone can season it to their liking. Tender beef also appears in the suyuk (boiled beef slices with dips) and what the restaurant calls lasagna dumplings: squares of dumpling stuffing with the wrapper on the top and bottom.

After a decades-long hustle, Burmese Bites chef and owner Myo Lin Thway has finally opened the full-service restaurant of his dreams. The former buffet-style Point Brazil in Astoria has transformed into a cool, bustling space with quick, kind service. All the bestsellers from Thway’s days at street festivals, Queens Night Market, and Queens Center Mall now rest in beautiful, colorful ceramics and thatched wood plateware. The must-orders: the assorted palatas like the chicken curry that kickstarted the business; tea leaf salad; ohno kauswe (coconut chicken noodle soup); mohinga (ground fish noodle soup); and crispy eel chile fries.

Xiaozhan is a fantastic rice noodle soup spot with a sauce bar in Flushing, which opened in May. All ten noodle soups are served in mini clay pots with bundles of slippery, slurpy, bouncy rice noodles; vegetables; and protein options such as fish, beef, shrimp, and chicken. The soup bases vary from mushrooms to assorted chile preparations (charred, pickled, oil), but the passionfruit stands out. It has a lovely balance of robust flavors — sour, spicy, savory — brightened up with passion fruit and lemon. And if you want more spiciness or umami, head to the sauce bar. The space is tiny, and wait times can exceed an hour, so go during off-peak hours.

Northwestern Queens can now grab some good Nigerian jollof and suya with the opening of the D.C.-based takeout chain Disbe Good, which opened inside the Sunnyside Eats ghost kitchen in May. The jollof is fluffy, tomato-based, and subtly spicy. But the charcoal-grilled smokiness of the suya is loud and proud — whether you opt for the beef, chicken, or lamb. And all the meats are halal. Every order comes with an extra helping of yaji, their quality suya spice blend of peanut, smoked paprika, and chile pepper, so you can use any leftovers for your own home cooking.

Woodside has gained a thoughtful restaurant that pushes the boundaries of typical Japanese American restaurants in New York with Tomoni, which opened in April. Lunch sets include common premium offerings like wagyu or eel donburi, but the perfectly cooked protein portions are generous. But Tomoni also offers misozuke cream cheese, which has been marinated in miso for two days and served with nori and wasabi; it’s delightful: nutty and slightly sweet. There’s also the raw octopus (a small bowl of shredded octopus in a slightly vinegary seasoning) and natto (the sticky, stringy fermented soybeans usually eaten at home). It’s served with rice, sauce, a raw pasteurized egg, a couple of slices of grilled eel, tamagoyaki, and miso soup.

What looks small and divey from the front opens up into a large Chinese banquet hall-type space. Peruse a massive menu of Cantonese classics that had been sorely missing in NYC’s newest Chinatown. Fresh lobster is coated in a garlicky brown sauce. Fried whole anchovies are tossed in salt and pepper. Stellar snow pea sprouts get braised in a light savory broth, topped with fried shrimp, and served in a cast iron pot. Head over for weekday lunch specials ($14-17) on entrees like beef stew with radish and chicken with cashews — all served with soup and rice.

A new Uzbek restaurant has been doling out traditional dishes in Rego Park since April. Registan Plov Center lives up to its name with a plov that’s freshly made daily in the mornings. It’s a dome of rice, chickpeas, lamb, and cubed carrots with pops of sweetness from raisins — all tantalizingly slicked with lamb fat. Get the grilled lamb ribs, too. It’s served on a mountain of sliced lemon and tomato, topped with potato chips and a flourish of sliced onions. Wash it all down with kompot, a light seasonal fruit juice; it’s mixed berries for summer.

On the weekends, all the Forest Hills families are at the massive new location of Turkish American chain Zara, which opened in May. Of the many highlights, the huge complimentary balloon bread — that’s the length of an arm and puffed up straight out of the open-flame oven — might be the greatest. Rip into it and dip into spreads like labneh, hummus, and babaganoush. Or wrap it around grilled kababs, short ribs, and steaks. Leave room for desserts. The tas kadayif is made fresh to order: pan-fried pastry stuffed with walnuts and honey, which is served with vanilla ice cream.

items.title: Must-Try Spots For Noodle Lovers
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In
items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”

Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.
2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam

Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.

At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.
3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan

This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.

You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. items.text:
Welcome to the Eater Cocktail Heatmap, focusing on the hottest new bar openings in New York every month.

Eater editors do thorough reporting on the most exciting restaurant openings to hit the city, as well as smaller openings worth having on the radar. In this monthly map, we narrow the field to cocktail bars that are drawing the most excitement, buzz, crowds, and early positive chatter, focusing on spots that have only been open for six months or less. When an Eater editor has already been to a place, we share insider tips on what to expect and what’s worth ordering as well.

New to the list in October: We’ve added Japanese cocktail bar Don’t Be Shy in Hudson Square; massive Chinese-leaning cocktail bar/restaurant/karaoke lounge Rewind in Long Island City; South Asian speakeasy Jam & Jaggery in the East Village; and retro bars FKA in the East Village and Velvet Cowboy on the Upper West Side. For now, we’ve removed Bar Chimera, Peek Inn, and Hidden Rivers Beer Garden.

For related drinking guides, check out Eater NY’s picks for the best cocktail bars, dive bars, and wine bars. And for more New York dining recommendations, check out the new hotspots in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens. In need of an insider’s perspective on how to eat well, no matter where you are in NYC? Pick up our book: The Eater Guide to New York City.

The Jacob’s Pickles team turned its space on the Upper West Side (which relocated to Columbus Avenue) into Velvet Cowboy, a new 1970s Southwestern cocktail bar, in September. Find $5 bar snacks, like a take on the McRib sandwich, chili-cheese fries, and a huge funnel cake hanging from a stand.

A massive new restaurant-cocktail bar-karaoke lounge, Rewind, opened in Long Island City this September and is co-founded with AYS Hospitality, which runs Mr. Moto’s restaurant portfolio. The drinks menu, developed by beverage director Ken Chen, who had been at Taipei gastropub Indulge Experimental Bistro, took cues from tea, the Chinese zodiac, and the five elements. Tipsy Blossom represents fire signs and bitter elements, made with whisky, shochu, chrysanthemum, pear, hawthorn, licorice root, and goji berry. The food menu includes truffle-mushroom congee, Taiwanese fried chicken, and wagyu donburi. Per the name, people enter the space by pressing a “rewind” button on a retro boombox outside.

The team behind West Village cocktail lounge Dandelion expanded with Keepers, a new neighborhood-leaning bar and pizzeria, in July. Drinks, courtesy of Ricky Dolinsky (formerly of the View), include interesting Negronis such as the Black Forest, a drinkable homage to Ben & Jerry’s Cherry Garcia; spritzes; and frozens. Food-wise, find crispy tavern pies.

Bernie and Herb’s comes from a trio of 169 Bar alums who wanted to do a neighborhood spot that’s affordable and stays open until late. The bar opened in July, housed in the space that had been part of Coffee Shop, the Brazilian late-night icon in the area for 30 years. Look for drinks around $10 and inexpensive bar food like hot dogs, pulled pork sandwiches, and more.

FKA, which stands for “Formerly Known As,” is all about retro vibes since it opened in September in the East Village. Look for dollar East Coast oysters; dishes like lamb tartare, pimento cheese, Frito pies, and cheeseburgers; activities like pinball and Big Buck Hunter; and drinks like strawberry daiquiris, natural wines, and $8 beer-and-shot combos.

Chef Aarthi Sampath debuted a new speakeasy underneath her East Village restaurant Drāvida in September. Jam & Jaggery takes on the same South Asian foundation, with drinks like the Dirty Currytini with olive vermouth and curry leaves, and the Gola Chaat with shochu, yogurt, pomegranate, tamarind, herbs, and aloo bhujia, the latter of which is a spiced boiled potato snack. Sampath is offering some of her upstairs snacks, along with an Indian-ish burger.

The team, whose bar history includes Bar Valentina and Employees Only, took over the former Bandits space with a French-leaning bar. Bar Etienne opened in the West Village in August, with a very banana-y rum cocktail along with tomato martinis, chocolate Negronis, and wines. The bistro food menu includes steak au poivre and French onion-grilled cheeses, plus desserts created in collaboration with nearby Claude Bakery, such as tarte tatin and that chocolate cake.

New Hudson Square cocktail bar Don’t Be Shy is meant to evoke Tokyo’s stylish Ginza district since it opened in September. Head bartender Shinya Yamao, who worked at now-closed Piora and Tribeca sake bar Shigure, developed a Japanese cocktail menu with a special Trip to Japan menu available only at the nine-seat bar counter, exploring Japanese history and regionality, like the Edo, made with a potato-miso-flavored vodka and a sweet potato-Campari ice cube. Other drinks are available at the table seats, such as the Miyajima, which has momo nigori sake, red shiso, and lemon. Food includes wagyu and egg salad sandos and umami burrata with taro chips, pecans, dashi, and tomato sorbet.

Alas, Enid’s isn’t coming back, but the Greenpoint Fish & Lobster team turned its Greenpoint address into a new bar paying tribute to another shuttered neighborhood fixture. They opened Matches (a nod to Bar Matchless) in August, with $16 cocktails, along with burgers and steak frites.

Co-owners and couple Mercury Tin and Philip Dizard opened Tin’s on the Lower East Side as their ode to their life experiences. It’s a two-floor, New York-meets-Shanghai bar and restaurant that opened in July (and thankfully, the kitchen is fully open, serving those Shanghai-style dumplings). Drinks pay homage to those blending influences; see: an ode to the Dead Rabbit’s Irish coffee with a Shanghai dirty coffee twist.

A new cocktail bar devoted to all things rum opened in Williamsburg in April in the former original Gertie space. Echo Lake offers $12 daily daiquiris and a lager/rum shot combo cutely called Tiny and a Tot, plus seafood-centric plates like oysters with tepache mignonette and green coconut curry chowder. The new bar comes from beverage power couple Chloe Frechette (the former executive editor at Eater sibling site Punch) and Paul McGee, who cut his teeth at Chicago’s now-closed tropical bar Lost Lake. The duo is also featuring their own collection of liquid loot within the intimate basement rum bar, Undercurrent.

The team behind Mexican fine-dining restaurant Corima and burrito hot spot Vato opened a new bar in downtown Manhattan this April. Bar Chucho, a comparatively casual bar counterpart to Corima, offers fantastic drinks like the Desert Rain with sotol, along with lots of micheladas and familiar food like the carne asada-esque burger.

New Williamsburg bar Dokidoki, which opened in July, is just a fun meshing of Latin and Japanese cultures, courtesy of co-owners and cocktail vets A-K Hada, an alum of Please Don’t Tell and Existing Conditions; and Christian Suzuki-Orellana, a semifinalist on Netflix’s Drink Masters. With just a beer and wine license, they’re whipping up fun martinis and honeydew “margaritas” made with shochu, sakes, and local meads. The Japanese-Puerto Rican-Salvadoran bar snacks include a katsu sandwich made with cod on shokupan bread. It’s a small yet cozy space.

Brooklyn cocktail bar Grand Army alums Patty Dennison and Ally Marrone opened their own bar in Williamsburg in May, taking over what was the Ensenada space. The press release describes Kinda Nice as a mix of “late-night diner culture” and “dive bar spontaneity,” which translates to savory and sweet cocktails like the guava Negroni with malted milk and pisco; the Greek Salad martini with Tomato Crop vodka and a piparra brine; and a tequila drink with lime sherbet and a choice of blueberry or strawberry amaro and tequila. The duo also debuted their downstairs dive bar at the address, Shenanigans, with beers, highballs, boilermakers, and DJs (dancing is encouraged)

New Bushwick bar the Museum Bar + Gift Shop is meant to feel like a hella fun natural history museum, which opened in June. The space is covered in illuminated fossils, crystals, and dinosaur heads. The drinks list continues that thread, with the Insectarium, a Negroni-ish drink with insects; and the Ocean Life made with rum, coconut, limes, Curaçao, and cuttlefish ink. The on-site Gift Shop bar focuses on lower-ABV drinks with cafe touches, such as spritzes and milk punches.

Billy Durney was inspired by “one crazy night in Paris many years ago” to open this Brooklyn cocktail bar next door to his Red Hook Tavern, with “reinvented disco-era cocktails,” in May. That translates to vibrant Blue Hawaiians, Adam’s Appletinis, and creamy White Russians and Brandy Alexanders. And yes, there’s an iteration of that famous cheeseburger, too.

This new Gowanus spot, which opened in July, aims to fill the bar gap left by the address’s previous tenant, Dirty Precious, now with a 1980s look. Co-owners Robin Daily and Mike Brown met at Royal Palms Shuffleboard Club, where one worked and the other frequented, respectively. At Shania’s Max Bet, they’re serving up martinis, Midori sours, and beer-shot combos.

It’s a horse girl’s world: Co-founders and couple Elana Shvalbe and Michael Furac opened this new daytime cafe and evening bar in Red Hook in August, with a pony-loving aesthetic. Find gin martinis; a rye-and-rum Old Fashioned with peanut butter and bananas; and a High Life pony-shot combo for $10, along with an Eastern European-ish food menu including pelmeni and cured and smoked fish.

More in Dining Out in NY

https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/Moonlit_Aroma_Rewind2611.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C27.766927083333%2C100%2C44.466145833333&w=2400

blocks.x: https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/rewind2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=16.644113667118%2C0%2C66.711772665765%2C100&w=2400
blocks.c: The Best New Restaurants in Queens

blocks.x: Bernie and Herb’s comes from a trio of 169 Bar alums who wanted to do a neighborhood spot that’s affordable and stays open until late. The bar opened in July, housed in the space that had been part of Coffee Shop, the Brazilian late-night icon in the area for 30 years. Look for drinks around $10 and inexpensive bar food like hot dogs, pulled pork sandwiches, and more.
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/07/Keepers_the-Classic-Black-Forest-Negroni_Noah-Fecks.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.035688793718776%2C100%2C99.928622412562&w=2400
blocks.c: Keepers_the Classic & Black Forest Negroni_Noah Fecks

blocks.x: FKA, which stands for “Formerly Known As,” is all about retro vibes since it opened in September in the East Village. Look for dollar East Coast oysters; dishes like lamb tartare, pimento cheese, Frito pies, and cheeseburgers; activities like pinball and Big Buck Hunter; and drinks like strawberry daiquiris, natural wines, and $8 beer-and-shot combos.
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/07/IMG_2342.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C35.046235375148%2C100%2C50&w=2400

Chef Aarthi Sampath debuted a new speakeasy underneath her East Village restaurant Drāvida in September. Jam & Jaggery takes on the same South Asian foundation, with drinks like the Dirty Currytini with olive vermouth and curry leaves, and the Gola Chaat with shochu, yogurt, pomegranate, tamarind, herbs, and aloo bhujia, the latter of which is a spiced boiled potato snack. Sampath is offering some of her upstairs snacks, along with an Indian-ish burger.
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/FKA-Food-Group-3_Photo-Credit-Sebastian-Lange.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.0099980003999178%2C100%2C99.9800039992&w=2400
blocks.c: FKA Food Group 3_Photo Credit Sebastian Lange

blocks.x: The team, whose bar history includes Bar Valentina and Employees Only, took over the former Bandits space with a French-leaning bar. Bar Etienne opened in the West Village in August, with a very banana-y rum cocktail along with tomato martinis, chocolate Negronis, and wines. The bistro food menu includes steak au poivre and French onion-grilled cheeses, plus desserts created in collaboration with nearby Claude Bakery, such as tarte tatin and that chocolate cake.
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/GOLA-CHAAT.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C29.000888211104%2C100%2C37.48427672956&w=2400
blocks.c: GOLA CHAAT

blocks.x: https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/BarEtienne-Martini-Tomate-and-French-Onion-Grilled-Cheese.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C6.5664370781696%2C100%2C83.320735701688&w=2400
blocks.c: BarEtienne- Martini Tomate and French Onion Grilled Cheese

blocks.x: New Hudson Square cocktail bar Don’t Be Shy is meant to evoke Tokyo’s stylish Ginza district since it opened in September. Head bartender Shinya Yamao, who worked at now-closed Piora and Tribeca sake bar Shigure, developed a Japanese cocktail menu with a special Trip to Japan menu available only at the nine-seat bar counter, exploring Japanese history and regionality, like the Edo, made with a potato-miso-flavored vodka and a sweet potato-Campari ice cube. Other drinks are available at the table seats, such as the Miyajima, which has momo nigori sake, red shiso, and lemon. Food includes wagyu and egg salad sandos and umami burrata with taro chips, pecans, dashi, and tomato sorbet.

Alas, Enid’s isn’t coming back, but the Greenpoint Fish & Lobster team turned its Greenpoint address into a new bar paying tribute to another shuttered neighborhood fixture. They opened Matches (a nod to Bar Matchless) in August, with $16 cocktails, along with burgers and steak frites.
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/09/IMG_8688.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C27.548191106491%2C100%2C58.394160583942&w=2400
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/07/Tins_Beverage_Max-Flatow-24.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.0032057446944975%2C100%2C99.993588510611&w=2400
blocks.c: Tin’s_Beverage_Max Flatow (24)

blocks.x: Co-owners and couple Mercury Tin and Philip Dizard opened Tin’s on the Lower East Side as their ode to their life experiences. It’s a two-floor, New York-meets-Shanghai bar and restaurant that opened in July (and thankfully, the kitchen is fully open, serving those Shanghai-style dumplings). Drinks pay homage to those blending influences; see: an ode to the Dead Rabbit’s Irish coffee with a Shanghai dirty coffee twist.

https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/03/Echo-Lake_Lost-Lake-cocktail_Photo-Credit-Lizzie-Munro.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0.0038092335822029%2C0%2C99.992381532836%2C100&w=2400
blocks.c: Echo Lake_Lost Lake cocktail_Photo Credit Lizzie Munro

blocks.x: A new cocktail bar devoted to all things rum opened in Williamsburg in April in the former original Gertie space. Echo Lake offers $12 daily daiquiris and a lager/rum shot combo cutely called Tiny and a Tot, plus seafood-centric plates like oysters with tepache mignonette and green coconut curry chowder. The new bar comes from beverage power couple Chloe Frechette (the former executive editor at Eater sibling site Punch) and Paul McGee, who cut his teeth at Chicago’s now-closed tropical bar Lost Lake. The duo is also featuring their own collection of liquid loot within the intimate basement rum bar, Undercurrent.
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/03/barc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C25%2C100%2C50&w=2400
blocks.c: barc

blocks.x: The team behind Mexican fine-dining restaurant Corima and burrito hot spot Vato opened a new bar in downtown Manhattan this April. Bar Chucho, a comparatively casual bar counterpart to Corima, offers fantastic drinks like the Desert Rain with sotol, along with lots of micheladas and familiar food like the carne asada-esque burger.
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/03/barc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C12.5%2C100%2C75&w=2400
blocks.c: One of NYC’s Most Fun New Bars Also Serves Good Food

blocks.x: New Williamsburg bar Dokidoki, which opened in July, is just a fun meshing of Latin and Japanese cultures, courtesy of co-owners and cocktail vets A-K Hada, an alum of Please Don’t Tell and Existing Conditions; and Christian Suzuki-Orellana, a semifinalist on Netflix’s Drink Masters. With just a beer and wine license, they’re whipping up fun martinis and honeydew “margaritas” made with shochu, sakes, and local meads. The Japanese-Puerto Rican-Salvadoran bar snacks include a katsu sandwich made with cod on shokupan bread. It’s a small yet cozy space.

https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/07/dokidoki-Coastline-Chronicles-photo-credit-Shannon-Sturgis.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.02939447383892%2C100%2C99.941211052322&w=2400

blocks.c: KindaNice_firstselects_May2026_ss-013

The press release describes Kinda Nice as a mix of “late-night diner culture” and “dive bar spontaneity,” which translates to savory and sweet cocktails like the guava Negroni with malted milk and pisco; the Greek Salad martini with Tomato Crop vodka and a piparra brine; and a tequila drink with lime sherbet and a choice of blueberry or strawberry amaro and tequila. The duo also debuted their downstairs dive bar at the address, Shenanigans, with beers, highballs, boilermakers, and DJs (dancing is encouraged)
https://platform.ny.eater.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/06/The-Museum-Bar-Gift-Shop-Interior-7-credit-Kyle-Berg.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400
blocks.c: The Museum Bar + Gift Shop - Interior 7 (credit Kyle Berg)

blocks.x: New Bushwick bar the Museum Bar + Gift Shop is meant to feel like a hella fun natural history museum, which opened in June. The space is covered in illuminated fossils, crystals, and dinosaur heads. The drinks list continues that thread, with the Insectarium, a Negroni-ish drink with insects; and the Ocean Life made with rum, coconut, limes, Curaçao, and cuttlefish ink. The on-site Gift Shop bar focuses on lower-ABV drinks with cafe touches, such as spritzes and milk punches.

items.title: London Is Calling at Soho’s Hot New Straker’s
items.summary:
Thomas Straker’s namesake London hit makes its stateside debut in NYC this weekend. | Thomas Streat/Straker’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the new
items.text:
Thomas Straker’s namesake London hit makes its stateside debut in NYC this weekend. | Thomas Streat/Straker’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the new restaurants, bars, and cafes that have opened this week in October 2026 Throughout the month, we’ll update the list weekly (see: September, August, July, June, May, April, March, February, January). When we’ve been to a place, we will then include a few openings on our heatmaps (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, cocktail bars) to let you know the ones we like. If there’s an opening in your neighborhood that we’ve missed, let us know at ny@eater.com.

October 7

Spotlight

Soho: London chef and internet butter evangelist Thomas Straker takes over the former Lucky Strike, Keith McNally’s now-closed Soho fixture, for his first restaurant outside the U.K. A late-September opening date for Straker’s was pushed back to Saturday, October 10. The New York restaurant centers on an open kitchen surrounded by steel and green stone, leather banquettes, dark wood, and warm lighting. Expect the modern British cooking style with Italian leanings that defines the Notting Hill original that opened in 2022. 59 Grand Street, at West Broadway

And the rest…

Brooklyn Heights: Brooklyn’s charming new Georgian restaurant Bebo, open since late September, pays homage to grandmas everywhere with comfort foods like khachapuri, vibrant dips, and crockets of soup in a cozy space surrounded by fringed lampshades, cottage curtains, and antique plateware. 145 Atlantic Avenue, between Henry and Clinton streets, Brooklyn

Bronx: After 14 years, neighborhood sports bar Triona’s closed its original location after the Chicago Bears game on Monday, September 28, but reopened next door on Friday, October 2, as Triona’s Vintage Sporting Club. The landmarked Scheffel Hall building dating back to the late-1800s was a German beer hall and restaurant and later housed the German-American Athletic Club and Fat Tuesday’s jazz club. Vintage sports memorabilia joins more than 20 screens and an updated Irish-leaning pub menu, with a continued love for the Bears and Michigan Wolverines. 190 Third Avenue, at East 17th Street

Chelsea: A chic taste of Verona landed in New York on Thursday, October 1, with the arrival of Italian wine bar and bistro Bar Lento. Lento, the Italian word for “slow,” features a brick-framed backdrop with a secret garden inside. The warm setup showcases a wine list of whites, bubbles, and pét-nats from Sardinia to Veneto to go along with seasonal plates like bruschetta and fluke ceviche in a citrus tomato vinaigrette. 158 Eighth Avenue, near West18th Street

Chinatown: Something Smells Fishy, a casual Japanese seafood counter that accepts walk-ins only, specializes in customizable kaisendon rice bowls topped with the likes of raw tuna, salmon, fluke, and uni. 95A Elizabeth Street, near Grand Street

Crown Heights: Brooklyn Surf & Soul, a new takeout spot serving seafood and soul food, opened on October 3. It’ll offer shrimp po’ boy sandwiches, whiting sandwiches, shrimp and grits, seafood boils, fried chicken, and more. 602 Nostrand Avenue, near Pacific Street

East Village: Table Mercato, Boston’s cult-favorite Italian sandwich shop that specializes in crispy chicken cutlets shoved between freshly baked focaccia, added its first NYC location in late September. Chef Jen Royle’s popular Sicilian and spicy vodka Parm sandwiches, priced in the mid-$20s a pop, commanded immediate long lines out front (open 11 a.m. until sell-out). There are also house-made chips, onion dip, and rainbow cookies. 214 E. 10th Street, between First and Second avenues

Financial District: Nationwide ramen bar Kyuramen debuted a trio of fast-casual spots on one 9-to-5 strip in NY on Thursday, October 1. Kyuramen Express slings ramen, udon, rice bowls, sushi, onigiri, and appetizers; Bao Dumpling is a Chinese takeout with a knack for dumplings; and Aokō Matcha offers specialty green drinks and desserts. Open daily from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. for dine-in, takeout, and delivery. 40 Gold Street, near Fulton Street

Lincoln Center: Prolific French chef Daniel Boulud returns across from NYC’s cultural hub in a big way on Thursday, October 8, with the opening of Brasserie Boulud — a consolidation of his closed Upper West Side restaurants (Bar Boulud, Boulud Sud, and Épicerie Boulud) into one massive, 10,000-square-foot flagship. The classically French-leaning Brasserie Boulud features the greatest hits from each dearly missed restaurant in one combined menu. Expect seafood towers, French onion soup, steak frites, lobster souffle, and boudin blanc, along with the return of Boulud’s cult-favorite DB Burger. 1900 Broadway, at Lincoln Plaza

Lower East Side: Australia’s popular and prolific Gelato Messina has made its American debut, with the opening of Softville on October 1. Continuing the city’s fancy soft serve moment, Softville will offer it, made using dairy from Ronnybrook Farm in the Hudson Valley, alongside an extensive and rotating menu of sauces and toppings. It also offers loaded sundaes, such as a birthday cake sundae featuring fior di latte soft serve, butter cake, strawberry pudding, “birthday crumble,” strawberry and white chocolate sauce, cream cheese chantilly cream, and sprinkles. A collaboration with Studio Jeremyville, the shop is described as an “art-led concept store,” in which Studio Jeremyville sculptures and other art will be on display. The art studio has worked with Messina since its early days, creating murals for its stores. 137 Orchard Street, between Rivington and Delancey streets

Lower East Side: Brazilian restaurant Iara opened on Friday, October 2, from chef Vitor Mendes, who previously worked at Brooklyn hot spot Theodora. Mendes cites a trip to his home country of Brazil following his father’s death as inspiration for the restaurant. Before it, he told Eater NY, “I thought that my own culture was rice, beans, and barbecue, as a lot of people might think.” At Iara, he’ll employ cassava in many ways: in the crispy cubes of tapioca served with yellowfin tuna and smoked biquinho peppers, in the vinaigrette paired with his hiramasi ceviche, in the fries that accompany his picanha, and more. 205 Allen Street, at East Houston Street

Park Slope: After shuttering his 120-year-old family bakery in Carroll Gardens earlier this spring, James Caputo is back in the baking business with Caputo Bagels, which opened Monday, October 5. The new bagel shop, a collaboration with Miriam owner Rafi Hasid next door, is all about hand-rolled sourdough bagels, open-face and breakfast sandwiches, as well a familiar take on the bake shop’s famed lard bread. 81 Fifth Avenue, near Prospect Place, Brooklyn

Red Hook: All-day diner and bar Vals debuted in Brooklyn at the beginning of October with a menu full of waffles, Denver omelets, blue-plate specials like spaghetti and meatballs, funnel cakes, and milkshakes. Located in the revived Fort Defiance, Vals’ name nods to the nearby Valentino Pier. Nicely priced drinks at the newly expanded bar include draft cocktails, well drinks, beer-shot combos, Negronis, martinis, and more. The new hangout comes from Victoria Viscusi, chef Allie Gassaway, and Laine Pelka, the latter two of which previously worked in the same space before. 347 Van Brunt Street, at Wolcott Street, Brooklyn

Theater District: Diner 24, the Gramercy greasy spoon known for its giant shakes, hot dogs, and burgers served by singing waiters, added a flagship corner location in the heart of Times Square on Wednesday, October 6. Located right under the historical Lambs clubhouse, the new 235-seat Diner 24 that’s open around the clock also hosts hourly performances from actors with Broadway backgrounds from a dedicated 20-foot stage upstairs. “Mamma Mia” and milkshakes, anyone? 1674 Broadway, at 52nd Street

Times Square: Southern food chain Kitchen + Kocktails by Kevin Kelley, which started in Dallas in 2020, opened its first location in New York City. The restaurant, which is the chain’s largest, will serve dishes such as Cajun crab cakes, fried seafood and chicken, smothered steak, jerk lamb chops, and shrimp and grits. The opening continues the restaurant’s national expansion. It also has locations in Atlanta, Charlotte, Chicago, Miami, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C., and will soon be opening in Boston and New Orleans. 7 Times Square, at 7th Avenue and 41st Street

West Village: Camari Mick’s long-awaited Calabash, billed as an Afro-Caribbean bakery and brasserie, opened for daytime service on Friday, October 2. Running from Thursday to Sunday, daytime service will feature Mick’s acclaimed baked goods, including sticky buns, coconut canelés, and beef patty croissants, plus cornbread pancakes with salted maple sabayon. Dinner service begins on October 9 and will be available for a single 6:30 p.m. seating on Friday and Saturday nights via prepaid bookings. It will offer dishes including suya steak frites using plantain fries and asun pasta with goat ragu and pappardelle. There’s no alcohol here, but there are fermented drinks and NA cocktails. 183 Christopher Street, near Weehawken Street

West Village: The team behind Zimmi’s expands next door on Wednesday, October 7, with the debut of a tiny 15-seat wine bar and cafe called Bar à Part. Look for small plates, an extensive wine list, as well as savory and sweet pastries from acclaimed pastry chef Clodagh Manning – the Ireland native who previously worked at London’s now-closed Lyle’s. 72 Bedford Street, at Commerce Street

Williamsburg: A new steakhouse landed in the neighborhood with the opening of Booth’s Extra Fine on October 6. The restaurant comes from the team behind Nobody Told Me; it gets its name from chef Nick Pfannersteil’s grandfather, Booth, a Milwaukee car salesman with a penchant for steak and martinis. The menu will feature the requisite steaks and martinis, plus horseradish burgers, truffle ravioli, pork chops, rum cherry sundaes, and more. A nightly Martini Hour from 4 to 6 p.m. will offer $12 martinis, $5 mini hot dogs, $2 oysters, and half-priced caviar. The location previously housed Mighty Quinn’s BBQ. 62 South 2nd Street, near Wythe Avenue

Upper East Side: Prolific Southern chicken chain Zaxbys made its Manhattan debut on Wednesday, September 30. Along with its breaded chicken “fingerz” and a dozen sauces, the menu includes Buffalo wings and a salad section it calls “zalads.” Atlanta-based Zaxbys, founded in 1990, has more than 1,000 locations across 24 states. Its only other NYC storefront sits in the Bronx. 1267 First Avenue, between 68th and 69th streets

Upper East Side: NoMad cocktail lounge Obvio – home to the New York Times’ “Martini of the Year” – starts a semi-permanent residency at its Upper East Side sibling Casa Cruz on Thursday, October 1. Every Thursday to Saturday night, the second floor of the Beaux-Arts mansion – redesigned with Obvio’s giraffe-patterned calling card – imports Obvio favorites like the Tamarind Mezcalito along with pisco-centric drink debuts like a Marmalade Martini from beverage director Amy Racine. Chef John Fraser’s popular tartare tacos and burger join new caviar cones stuffed with Toro tuna. 36 E. 61st Street, between Park and Madison avenues
